lines.text: Source: Microsoft Learn - Install WSL URL:
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install Use: Current install/verify guidance:
prerequisites, wsl --install, wsl --list --verbose, WSL 2. Use only for setup truth; the course owns
workspace practice.
Why this matters
A beginner can have Python installed and still be blocked by a sentence such as "run this in
Linux," "use Bash," or "clone it inside WSL." Windows and Linux are not two mysterious
competing computers. WSL gives you a Linux environment on your Windows machine. For this
course, the important skill is knowing which environment and filesystem you are using
before you install packages, create a repository or run a command.
Picture it in your head
Think of your laptop as one house with two workrooms. Windows has paths such as
C:\Users\.... Your Linux distribution has a Linux home such as /home/ashish. WSL can see
Windows files through mounts such as /mnt/c/..., but that does not mean every project should
live there. For Linux-heavy developer tools, keeping the working repository inside the Linux
filesystem (~/de-study/...) usually gives a simpler Unix permission/path model. Files you
merely want to exchange with Windows can still be reached through /mnt/c.
WSL is the Windows feature. WSL 2 is its current virtualized architecture. Ubuntu is a Linux
distribution you may run inside it. Bash is a shell that accepts commands inside Linux. These are
different layers; saying "I opened WSL" is often shorthand for "I opened my Ubuntu shell under
WSL."
Follow with me once
First, in Windows PowerShell, inspect rather than reinstall blindly:
wsl --status
wsl --list --verbose
If WSL is not installed, Microsoft's current route is an Administrator PowerShell with wsl
--install, followed by a restart. Do not keep rerunning install commands if WSL is already
present. The exact current Microsoft page is linked above because setup behavior can change.
Then open your Linux distribution and run:
whoami
uname -a
pwd
printf 'HOME=%s\n' "$HOME"
ls -la
pwd answers "where am I?" It does not mean "show all files." $HOME is your Linux user's home
directory. Create the course workspace only after you have proved where you are:
mkdir -p ~/de-study/M06
cd ~/de-study/M06
pwd
Expected shape: /home/<your-linux-user>/de-study/M06, not a random Windows download
path and not /root.
Now deliberately look at the Windows mount without moving your project there:
ls /mnt/c/Users
You have just proved the boundary instead of guessing it.
A failure worth understanding
If wsl --list --verbose shows version 1 for the distribution, that is not the same as "WSL is
broken." Record the actual state and use Microsoft's current upgrade guidance. If the Linux
prompt says you are root, stop and understand why before building a learner workspace there;
ordinary study should run as your normal Linux user.
If a command works in PowerShell but not Bash, or vice versa, ask first: which shell am I in?
Do not solve that by randomly reinstalling Python/Git in both places.
You do it alone
Create ~/de-study/M06/DE06-01-first-attempt/. Save a short environment.txt containing
the observed Linux username, pwd, kernel/WSL information, and a one-sentence statement of
where your future M06 repositories will live. Also write one Windows path and its WSL
/mnt/c/... equivalent.
Validate before moving on
You can explain WSL vs WSL2 vs Ubuntu vs Bash; prove whether your distro is WSL2; identify
your Linux home; and distinguish a Linux path from the mounted Windows path. You have not
claimed that installation succeeded unless you actually observed it on your PC.
Changed retry
Without rereading your first commands, open a fresh Linux shell, navigate from $HOME to a new
~/de-study/M06-retry folder, create it if missing, and state whether
C:\Users\YourName\Desktop is a valid Bash path. Then show the corresponding /mnt/c/...
form.
Evidence to keep
Prove WSL/distro/workspace state on your own PC; save observed commands and choose a
Linux-home M06 workspace. Preserve the first attempt, observed output/error, one independent
validation, and your own-words teach-back. If review is used, keep the changed retry separately.
Source: freeCodeCamp - Command Line Basics for Beginners (2026) URL:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mABpAI-pCw0 Use: 02:56-30:18: command line mental
model, ls, navigation, touch/rm, mkdir/rmdir.
Why this matters
Data engineering scripts constantly create folders, inspect files, move outputs and clean
temporary work. The danger is not that cd is difficult. The danger is acting in the wrong
directory or using a destructive command before you have inspected what it will affect.
Picture it in your head
Your terminal always has a current working directory. Relative paths start from that point;
absolute paths start from /. If you say data/orders.csv, Linux resolves it relative to where you
currently are. If you say /home/ashish/de-study/M06/data/orders.csv, the starting point is
explicit.
Imagine a warehouse worker with a trolley. pwd tells the worker which aisle they stand in. ls
inspects the shelf. cd moves to another aisle. cp makes another item. mv changes its location or
name. rm destroys the named item; there is no ordinary recycle-bin promise in a shell workflow.
Follow with me once
Copy the supplied data folder into your learner-owned sandbox, then work only there. Use a
fresh directory such as:
mkdir -p ~/de-study/M06/linux-sandbox
cd ~/de-study/M06/linux-sandbox
pwd
Create a small tree:
mkdir -p raw processed evidence
printf 'batch_id=B001\n' > raw/batch.txt
touch evidence/notes.txt
find . -maxdepth 2 -type f -print
Before every move, predict the resulting path:
cp raw/batch.txt processed/batch_copy.txt
mv processed/batch_copy.txt processed/B001.txt
ls -l raw processed
The original raw/batch.txt still exists because cp copied. mv renamed the copy; it did not
create a second one.
Try paths deliberately:
cd raw
cat batch.txt
cat ../processed/B001.txt
cd ..
.. means the parent directory. . means the current directory. ~ expands to your Linux home.
Now inspect before deleting:
ls -l processed/B001.txt
rm processed/B001.txt
ls -l processed
This is safe because you created the sandbox and inspected the exact file first. Do not practice
rm -rf on your home directory, a course master folder or a path assembled from an unverified
variable.
The space-in-a-name trap
This command has two arguments, not one filename:
cat monthly report.txt
If the file is really named monthly report.txt, quote it:
cat 'monthly report.txt'
Better engineering habit: prefer simple predictable names in project automation so quoting bugs
are less likely.
You do it alone
Inside a new DE06-02-first-attempt folder, create incoming, archive, and evidence. Create
two tiny files, copy one to archive, rename the other, then move it. Save a terminal transcript or
typed record that shows pwd before and after. Explain which commands changed content, which
changed location/name, and which merely inspected state.
Validate before moving on
You can navigate without repeatedly opening File Explorer, predict relative paths, distinguish
copy from move, and show exactly what an rm command will target before you run it.
Changed retry
Start from $HOME, create a different tree M06-retry/source and M06-retry/ready, then copy
notes.txt using an absolute source path and relative destination path. Prove both files exist
afterward. Delete only the retry copy after inspecting it.
Evidence to keep
Build a safe folder tree, copy/move/rename files, and explain relative vs absolute paths before
deleting a disposable file. Preserve the first attempt, observed output/error, one independent
validation, and your own-words teach-back. If review is used, keep the changed retry separately.
Source: freeCodeCamp - Command Line Basics for Beginners (2026) URL:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mABpAI-pCw0 Use: 30:18-43:32: echo/cat and file
inspection. Course adds pipes, stderr, grep, wc, head/tail and validation.
Why this matters
A terminal becomes powerful when commands can be connected. Instead of manually opening a
50,000-line log, you can read a stream, filter it, count it and send a result to another file. The
same idea later appears in data pipelines: one stage emits output that another stage consumes.
Picture it in your head
A normal command has three standard channels: stdin (input), stdout (normal output), and
stderr (error output). A pipe | sends stdout from the command on the left into stdin of the
command on the right. > writes stdout to a file and overwrites that file. >> appends. 2>
redirects stderr.
Do not memorize symbols as punctuation. Ask: "Which stream is moving where?"
Follow with me once
Work on a copy of data/pipeline.log and data/linux_orders.csv:
cat pipeline.log
head -n 2 pipeline.log
tail -n 2 pipeline.log
wc -l pipeline.log
grep 'WARN' pipeline.log
Now connect stages:
grep 'INFO' pipeline.log | wc -l
The first command emits matching INFO lines. The pipe feeds those lines to wc -l, which counts
them. If you later change the file, the answer changes because the command is operating on
current data.
Create evidence safely:
grep 'WARN' pipeline.log > warnings.txt
cat warnings.txt
grep 'INFO' pipeline.log >> warnings.txt
After >, warnings.txt contains the new output instead of its previous contents. After >>, new
output is added to the end. This distinction matters when a pipeline output must be
deterministic: accidental append can duplicate prior-run output.
Now separate errors:
cat file_that_does_not_exist.txt 2> error.txt
cat error.txt
The command failed, but the error was captured from stderr. In real automation you should also
inspect the command's exit code, which comes in DE06-12.
For CSV inspection, do not pretend grep is a CSV parser. It is useful for quick textual inspection,
not for safely parsing quoted commas. You already learned proper CSV parsing in M05. Use
terminal tools for questions suited to text streams, and Python for structured parsing.
History as evidence, not magic
Use history | tail to inspect recent commands on shells that support it. Shell history can
help reproduce what you typed, but it is not a reliable project README: histories can be cleared,
contain secrets, and differ across machines. Promote important commands into documented
scripts or README instructions.
You do it alone
Using your own copy of pipeline.log, produce three files: warn_only.txt, info_count.txt,
and missing_file_error.txt. Before each redirection, state whether the operation should
overwrite or append. Then answer: why would >> be dangerous in a daily report that is
supposed to be regenerated from scratch?
Validate before moving on
You can trace a pipeline left-to-right, distinguish stdout from stderr, show the difference
between > and >>, and refuse to use grep as a substitute for structured CSV parsing.
Changed retry
On a new small text file, count only lines containing Completed, save the count to a fresh output
file, deliberately run one failing cat, redirect only its stderr, and prove the normal count file was
not polluted by the error message.
Evidence to keep
Use pipes/redirection to create filtered/count/error evidence while distinguishing stdout, stderr,
overwrite and append. Preserve the first attempt, observed output/error, one independent
validation, and your own-words teach-back. If review is used, keep the changed retry separately.
Source: DigitalOcean - Essential Linux Commands (current reference) URL:
https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials/linux-commands Use: Use only the
sudo/chmod/chown/permission sections as current command reference. The learner book
remains authoritative for least-privilege reasoning and the safe practice task.
Why this matters
Linux permissions are one of the first places where beginners solve a small problem with a
dangerously large hammer. "Permission denied" does not automatically mean "use sudo," and
chmod 777 is not a professional universal fix. You need enough permission reasoning to work
safely without becoming a Linux administrator.
Picture it in your head
A typical ls -l line begins with permission bits for owner, group, and others. The letters are r
read, w write, and x execute. A regular shell script can contain perfect text and still refuse
./script.sh if the execute bit is not set.
sudo means "run this command with elevated privileges according to system policy." It changes
the authority of the command, not the correctness of your idea. If your path is wrong, sudo can
make a wrong destructive command more powerful.
Follow with me once
Create a harmless script in your sandbox:
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\necho safe-run\n' > hello.sh
ls -l hello.sh
Try:
./hello.sh
If the file lacks execute permission, Bash may report permission denied. Inspect first, then add
only the permission you need:
chmod u+x hello.sh
ls -l hello.sh
./hello.sh
u+x means "add execute permission for the owner." It is much more informative than giving
everyone every permission.
Compare:
bash hello.sh
./hello.sh
The first asks Bash to read the file as a script; the second asks the operating system to execute
the file directly, so the execute bit and shebang matter.
For package management, understand the lifecycle before typing commands:
sudo apt update
apt list --upgradable 2>/dev/null | head
apt update refreshes package metadata; it does not mean "upgrade everything." Only install
packages the current course step actually requires. Record what you installed and why.
A permission-denied recovery ladder
1. Read the exact error and path.
2. pwd and ls -l the target.
3. Ask whether you own the file and whether the operation genuinely needs elevated privileges.
4. Change the smallest relevant permission or path.
5. Use sudo only when the system-level operation legitimately requires it.
Never solve a course-project permission problem by recursively changing permissions on /,
/home, or a broad Windows mount.
You do it alone
Create DE06-04-first-attempt/run_check.sh without execute permission, capture the failed
direct-execution output, inspect its mode, then add only owner execute and rerun. Write three
sentences explaining why chmod 777 would be an unjustified response.
Validate before moving on
You can read the basic rwx groups, distinguish running a script through Bash from executing it,
and explain why elevated permission is a risk boundary.
Changed retry
Create a second script and make it executable with a symbolic mode change. Then remove only
owner execute, prove direct execution fails, and restore it. Do not use numeric 777 at any point.
Evidence to keep
Diagnose a permission-denied script, add only owner execute, and explain why sudo/777 are not
default fixes. Preserve the first attempt, observed output/error, one independent validation, and
your own-words teach-back. If review is used, keep the changed retry separately.
Source: freeCodeCamp - Git & GitHub Crash Course for Beginners [2026] URL:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mAFoROnOfHs Use:
01:04-05:41 - bounded mental-model visual onl
Git command practice is taught by learner book/lab.
Why this matters
Git is often taught as a spell: add, commit, push. That creates confusion as soon as git status
shows three kinds of state. Git becomes much easier when you understand the three local areas
first: working tree, staging area/index, and committed history.
Picture it in your head
Imagine editing a report at your desk. The working tree is what is currently on the desk. The
staging area is the exact set of changes you have selected for the next photograph. A commit is
the photograph plus metadata and a parent link. GitHub is not part of this three-area local
model; a remote comes later.
git add does not "upload." git commit does not "send to GitHub." git status is your
dashboard between each step.
Follow with me once
Create a learner-owned repository:
mkdir -p ~/de-study/M06/git-state-lab
cd ~/de-study/M06/git-state-lab
git init
git config user.name 'Your Name'
git config user.email 'you@example.com'
printf '# Pipeline Notes\n' > README.md
git status
README is untracked. Stage it deliberately:
git add README.md
git status
git diff --staged
Now the next commit snapshot contains README. Commit:
git commit -m 'Add pipeline notes README'
git log --oneline --decorate -5
Modify the file:
printf 'Input: orders.csv\n' >> README.md
git diff
git diff shows working-tree changes that are not staged. Stage them, then change the file
again:
git add README.md
printf 'Output: summary.json\n' >> README.md
git status
git diff
git diff --staged
This is a crucial moment: the staged snapshot and the current working file are now different. If
you commit now, only the staged version enters that commit. This is why "I ran git add earlier"
does not mean all later edits are staged.
Commit quality
A commit should represent one understandable change. "stuff", "final", and "update2" hide
intent. A useful message here could be Document input contract. A large data-engineering
project becomes debuggable when history explains decisions.
You do it alone
Build a new repository with README.md and pipeline.py. Make one commit for the README and
another for a small Python placeholder. Before each commit save: git status, git diff, and
git diff --staged. Explain in your own words which content will enter each commit and which
will not.
Validate before moving on
Given any git status, you can point to working-tree, staged and committed state. You can
prove a commit exists in git log and explain why a commit is not the same thing as a GitHub
upload.
Changed retry
In a fresh repository, stage a file, edit it again after staging, and predict what the commit will
contain. Commit, then prove the unstaged second edit remains in the working tree.
Evidence to keep
Create a repo and prove working tree -> staging -> commit state with status/diff/staged-diff/log
evidence. Preserve the first attempt, observed output/error, one independent validation, and
your own-words teach-back. If review is used, keep the changed retry separately.
Source: freeCodeCamp - Git & GitHub Crash Course for Beginners [2026] URL:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mAFoROnOfHs Use: 40:58-52:13: branches, checkout,
merge and merge-conflict resolution.
Why this matters
Branches let you develop a change without pretending the main line is already correct. Merge
conflicts are not Git "breaking." A conflict means Git cannot safely decide how to combine
competing edits. Your job is to understand the intended final state, not merely remove the scary
markers.
Picture it in your head
A branch name is a movable label pointing at a commit. When you commit on
feature/quality, that label moves forward. main stays where it was until you merge or
otherwise move it. A merge combines histories. If both sides changed the same nearby lines
differently, Git pauses and asks you to resolve the content.
Follow with me once
Use a disposable lab repository. Start with:
stage=raw
Commit it on main. Create and switch to a branch:
git switch -c feature/quality
Change the same line to:
stage=quality
Commit. Switch back to main and change it instead to:
stage=validated
Commit. Now:
git merge feature/quality
Git should stop with a conflict. Inspect:
git status
cat pipeline.txt
You will see conflict markers similar to <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>. These markers are
evidence of two competing versions. Do not choose a side just because it is labelled HEAD.
Decide the business-intended final state, for example:
stage=validated_quality
Remove the markers by editing the file to that deliberate state, then:
git add pipeline.txt
git status
git commit -m 'Resolve pipeline stage conflict'
The important evidence is not "merge succeeded." It is: what did each side mean, what final
content did you choose, and why?
Fast-forward vs merge commit
If main has not moved since your branch split, Git may fast-forward the label instead of creating
a merge commit. That is normal. Do not force a conflict merely to get a "more advanced"
history. In this lesson we deliberately create one conflict only so you can learn the recovery
process safely.
You do it alone
Create a fresh repo with a small config.txt. Make a feature branch and main branch alter the
same setting differently. Save pre-merge log, conflict output, conflicted file, your reasoning
note, resolved file, and post-merge log.
Validate before moving on
You can explain branch as a pointer, not a full copy; show which branch you are on; distinguish
fast-forward from conflict; and resolve conflict content based on intended behavior.
Changed retry
Create a conflict in a README run command. One branch says python app.py; the other says
python3 app.py --input data.csv. Resolve it to the command that matches the actual
project interface, then prove the command works. The answer must come from the project
contract, not from choosing "ours" or "theirs" mechanically.
Evidence to keep
Create and resolve a real same-line conflict based on intended final behavior; preserve
before/after evidence. Preserve the first attempt, observed output/error, one independent
validation, and your own-words teach-back. If review is used, keep the changed retry separately.
Source: freeCodeCamp - Git & GitHub Crash Course for Beginners [2026] URL:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mAFoROnOfHs Use:
55:50-1:00:24 - bounded push/fetch/pull visual.
Local-vs-remote reasoning is taught by learner book/lab.
Why this matters
A remote repository introduces a second copy of project history. Many beginners treat push,
fetch and pull as synonyms for "sync." They are not. You need to know which direction data
moves and whether your current branch is changed automatically.
Picture it in your head
Your local repository has local branches such as main. A remote named origin is just a
configured address. Git also keeps remote-tracking references such as origin/main, which
record the remote state you last learned about.
• push: send local commits to a remote branch (subject to permissions/rules).
• fetch: download remote commits/references; it does not merge them into your current
branch.
• pull: fetch and then integrate according to configured behavior. Because it combines steps,
you should know what you expect before using it.
Follow with me once - no GitHub account required
The supplied practice/run_local_git_lab.sh creates a bare local repository that acts like
a remote, pushes to it, and clean-clones from it. This proves Git remote mechanics without
internet credentials. Run it from a Linux shell:
bash practice/run_local_git_lab.sh ~/de-study/M06/local-remote-lab
When it prints LOCAL_GIT_LAB_PASS, inspect the learner clone:
cd ~/de-study/M06/local-remote-lab/learner
git remote -v
git branch -vv
git log --oneline --decorate --graph --all -10
The remote is local, but the concepts are real: origin points elsewhere, your branch can track a
remote branch, and a clean clone reconstructs committed/tracked state.
Follow with me once - GitHub mode
When you use your own GitHub repository, create an empty repository or follow the exact
GitHub UI state you actually see. Add it as a remote only after verifying the URL:
git remote add origin <your-repository-url>
git remote -v
git push -u origin main
Do not paste credentials into a remote URL, README or terminal transcript. Authentication
methods can change; follow GitHub's current authentication UI/docs.
To understand fetch, make a remote-side change through another clone or GitHub, then:
git fetch origin
git status -sb
git log --oneline --decorate --all -8
Your local main does not silently become the fetched commit just because origin/main moved.
You do it alone
Use either your own GitHub repo plus the local lab, or the local lab alone if credentials/network
are unavailable. Produce evidence for remote -v, tracking branch, one push, one fetch where
you explain what changed, and one clean clone. Label offline/local simulation honestly.
Validate before moving on
You can explain origin, local branch, remote-tracking branch, push, fetch and pull without
saying "they all sync." You never fabricate a GitHub push screenshot when you only used a local
bare remote.
Changed retry
Use a second bare remote and two clones. Make a commit in clone A, push it, then fetch from
clone B. Before merging/pulling in B, prove the working file has not changed while origin/main
has advanced.
Evidence to keep
Prove local/remote/tracking state using a local bare remote and real GitHub only if actually
available. Preserve the first attempt, observed output/error, one independent validation, and
your own-words teach-back. If review is used, keep the changed retry separately.
Source: GitHub Docs - Pull request quickstart URL:
https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/get-started/pull-request-quickstart Use:
Current GitHub PR workflow reference; learner book/lab own review evidence.
Offline fallback is explicitly allowed.
Why this matters
A pull request is where version control becomes a team decision. It is not "another Git
command." It is a review object hosted by platforms such as GitHub: proposed branch changes,
their diff, discussion, checks and merge decision.
Picture it in your head
Imagine main as a protected published route and your feature branch as a proposed detour. A
pull request says: "Here is the exact diff I want to merge, here is why, please review it."
Reviewers can comment, approve or request changes. Further commits to the branch update
the PR.
GitHub's current quickstart follows the same chain you should learn: branch/fork -> edit ->
commit -> push -> open PR -> request review -> address feedback -> merge or close.
Follow with me once
On a small repository, create a branch with one focused change:
git switch -c feature/add-validation-note
# edit README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m 'Document validation control'
git push -u origin feature/add-validation-note
Before opening the PR, inspect locally:
git diff main...HEAD
Your PR description should answer:
1. What changed?
2. Why is it needed?
3. How did you validate it?
4. What risk or limitation remains?
Do not write "please merge" with no evidence.
In GitHub, inspect the Files changed tab. A PR is partly a human-readable review of that diff. If
review finds a problem, edit locally, commit a repair, and push the same branch; GitHub updates
the PR. You do not need a new PR for each repair to that proposal.
Review decisions
Current GitHub reviews distinguish general comment, approve, and request changes. A
self-review is not equivalent to an independent teammate review, but for a solo portfolio it is still
useful to write a deliberate review note that identifies one risk and verifies the diff. Never claim
"peer reviewed" unless another person actually reviewed it.
You do it alone
If GitHub is available, open a PR for a small M06 repository change. Save the PR URL,
description, diff summary, one review/comment event, any repair commit, and final merge/close
decision. If GitHub is unavailable, build a local "PR simulation" note from git diff
main...feature and clearly label it OFFLINE REVIEW PRACTICE - NOT A GITHUB PR.
Validate before moving on
You can distinguish branch, commit, push and PR; explain why a PR is useful even when Git can
merge locally; and prove that review feedback maps to a specific diff/commit.
Changed retry
Review a changed branch where .env was accidentally added. Do not merge. Explain the
required response: remove/stop tracking the file, protect future tracking, and rotate any real
credential if it was exposed. Then verify the proposed diff no longer contains the secret file.
Evidence to keep
Open/review a real PR when available or honestly labelled offline review practice; connect
feedback to specific diff. Preserve the first attempt, observed output/error, one independent
validation, and your own-words teach-back. If review is used, keep the changed retry separately.
Source: Python 3.14 docs - venv URL: https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html Use: Current
virtual-environment behavior: isolated packages, disposable/recreatable environments, create
with python -m venv.
Why this matters
A repository should describe a project, not depend on whichever Python packages happen to be
installed globally on your laptop. A virtual environment gives the project an isolated package
environment that can be deleted and recreated.
Picture it in your head
Your source code belongs in the repository. .venv is a local tool-room built for that project. It
may contain many generated files and machine-specific paths; it is not the project itself.
Python's current documentation explicitly treats virtual environments as disposable/recreatable
and not something to check into source control.
Follow with me once
Inside a project repository:
python3 --version
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python --version
python -m pip --version
The shell prompt often changes, but do not use prompt decoration as your only proof. Inspect:
python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)'
It should point inside .venv.
Add .venv/ to .gitignore and verify:
printf '.venv/\n' >> .gitignore
git status --short
git check-ignore -v .venv/pyvenv.cfg
The environment can be rebuilt; your repository should record required
dependencies/configuration through appropriate project files, not ship your personal
environment directory.
For this module's standard-library sample project, requirements.txt deliberately contains no
third-party dependency. That is valid: do not install random packages merely to make the file
non-empty.
Activation is convenience, not magic
Activation modifies shell environment so python/pip resolve to the virtual environment. You can
also call its interpreter explicitly. The important question is which interpreter you are using, not
whether the prompt shows parentheses.
You do it alone
In a fresh repository, create .venv, prove its interpreter path, add the ignore rule, and
demonstrate that .venv is not staged by git add .. Deactivate, delete .venv, recreate it, and
prove the project still runs using only documented steps.
Validate before moving on
You can explain why .venv should not be committed, prove which interpreter is active, and
recreate the environment from repository instructions.
Changed retry
Create a second project environment named .venv, install no third-party package, then show
that deleting the environment does not delete your source. Recreate it and run the same script
from a fresh shell.
Evidence to keep
Create, ignore, delete and recreate .venv; prove project source remains reproducible. Preserve
the first attempt, observed output/error, one independent validation, and your own-words
teach-back. If review is used, keep the changed retry separately.
Source: freeCodeCamp - Git & GitHub Crash Course for Beginners [2026] URL:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mAFoROnOfHs Use:
OPTIONAL visual - no verified bounded range; Git hygiene context only.
Why this matters
Repositories are easy to copy, fork and publish. A secret committed once can escape far beyond
your laptop. .gitignore helps prevent unwanted untracked files from entering future
commits, but it is not a time machine and not a credential-revocation system.
Picture it in your head
Think of .gitignore as a doorman checking untracked files before Git starts tracking them. If a
file is already tracked, adding its name to .gitignore does not make Git forget its history. If a
real password/token has been exposed, removing the file from the next commit does not make
that credential safe again; rotate/revoke it.
Follow with me once
A basic project ignore file might contain:
.venv/
__pycache__/
.env
output/
*.log
Create a fake, clearly non-secret .env only for the lab:
printf 'DEMO_TOKEN=not-a-real-secret\n' > .env
git status --short
git check-ignore -v .env
It should be ignored. Create .env.example with variable names/placeholders only and
intentionally track that:
printf 'DEMO_TOKEN=replace_me_locally\n' > .env.example
git add .gitignore .env.example
git diff --staged
Before every push, git status and git diff --staged are cheap secret-hygiene controls.
The already-tracked trap
If a harmless demo file was already committed, adding it to .gitignore will not stop Git from
tracking it. git rm --cached <file> can remove it from the current tracked set while keeping
a local copy, but historical commits still exist. For a real secret, your first operational response
is credential rotation/revocation. History cleaning is a separate incident-handling task and may
require coordination.
Never paste real tokens into screenshots, terminal transcripts, course answers or AI prompts for
"debugging."

commit.
Validate before moving on
You can explain what .gitignore does and does not do, prove ignored state, and state the
correct response to an exposed real credential: rotate/revoke first, then repair repository/history

Source: Official Git docs - reset, restore, revert and reflog URL: https://git-scm.com/docs/git
Use: Use the official distinction between restore/revert/reset; pair with git-reflog docs. Course
lab focuses safe recovery rather than history tricks.
Why this matters
Undo commands are dangerous when chosen by memory instead of state. A professional asks
two questions first: Is the bad change committed? and Has the commit been
shared/published? The safest tool depends on that answer.
Picture it in your head
• git restore <file>: repair working-tree content from a selected source; it does not create a
new history commit by itself.
• git revert <commit>: create a new commit that reverses an earlier commit. This is often
appropriate for published/shared history because it preserves the record.
• git reflog: your local record of where references/HEAD recently pointed; useful when you
think a commit was "lost." Reflogs are local, not a remote backup.
• git reset can move branch history and may discard state depending on mode. It is not our
default beginner repair tool.
Follow with me once - restore
Modify a tracked file incorrectly but do not commit it:
git status
git diff -- README.md
git restore README.md
git status
You intentionally discard that uncommitted modification. This is why you inspect the diff first:
restore can remove work you wanted.
Follow with me once - revert
Make a disposable bad commit, for example changing a threshold from 100 to 999. Save its
hash:
git log --oneline -3
Then:
git revert <bad-commit-hash>
Inspect the new log. The bad commit still exists, followed by a new commit that reverses its
patch. History tells the truth about what happened.
Follow with me once - reflog
Switch branches and make several commits, then inspect:
git reflog --oneline -10
Reflog entries show recent HEAD/reference movement. If you accidentally moved a branch and
can no longer see a commit in ordinary git log, reflog can help identify the old commit ID so
you can create a recovery branch/tag before doing anything else.
Recovery decision before command
1. Save current git status, diff and log/reflog evidence.
2. Decide whether state is uncommitted, locally committed, or shared.
3. Choose the narrowest repair.
4. Re-run the project or validation after repair.
5. Explain what history changed.
You do it alone
In a disposable repository, prove all three: restore an uncommitted change after inspecting it;
create/revert a bad commit; and use reflog to locate a prior HEAD position. Save before/after
logs. Do not use reset --hard in the exercise.
Validate before moving on
You can choose restore vs revert based on state and explain reflog as a local recovery record,
not "Git backup in the cloud."
Changed retry
Create a new bad commit on a feature branch, pretend it was already shared, and use revert
rather than rewriting it away. Then deliberately detach/switch around and use reflog to identify
an earlier commit, creating recovery-check branch at that commit without deleting current
work.
Evidence to keep
Demonstrate restore, revert and reflog recovery in a disposable repository without reset --hard.
Preserve the first attempt, observed output/error, one independent validation, and your
own-words teach-back. If review is used, keep the changed retry separately.
Source: freeCodeCamp - Bash Scripting Tutorial for Beginners URL:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tK9Oc6AEnR4 Use:
OPTIONAL visual - no verified bounded range.
Use only for Bash context; book + shell lab required.
Why this matters
A shell script turns a remembered terminal sequence into an executable contract. Data pipelines
and deployment jobs use exit codes to decide whether a step succeeded. A script that prints
"error" but exits zero can fool an orchestrator into treating failure as success.
Picture it in your head
A script is a small program run by a shell. The shebang identifies the intended interpreter when
the script is executed directly. Environment variables carry external configuration. Positional
arguments provide invocation-specific input. Exit code 0 conventionally signals success;
non-zero signals failure.
Follow with me once
Inspect the supplied practice/run_exit_code_lab.sh:
bash practice/run_exit_code_lab.sh
printf 'exit=%s\n' "$?"
With no argument it should fail non-zero. Now:
bash practice/run_exit_code_lab.sh data/linux_orders.csv
printf 'exit=%s\n' "$?"
It should print a line count and exit 0.
A robust small wrapper can start with:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
But do not copy set -euo pipefail as superstition. Roughly: -e stops on many unhandled
command failures, -u treats unset variables as errors, and pipefail lets a pipeline report
failure if an earlier stage failed. Shell edge cases exist, so you still need explicit validation
around important boundaries.
Use variables safely:
if [ -z "$input" ]; then
echo 'usage: run.sh INPUT_FILE' >&2
exit 2
fi
Quote variable expansions such as "$input" so spaces/globbing do not silently turn one path
into several arguments.
Environment-driven configuration example:
: "${APP_ENV:=development}"
echo "environment=$APP_ENV"
Do not print secret variables for debugging.

configuration/input, invoke the sample Python project, return non-zero on failure, and print a
short safe success summary. Test success, missing variable, and missing-file paths. Record each
exit code.
Validate before moving on
A calling script can tell success from failure using the exit status; your wrapper quotes paths; no
secret is printed; and a missing required input fails before downstream work begins.

Use: Clone into a genuinely fresh folder. Course defines the reproducibility/handoff proof and

Why this matters
A repository is not truly reproducible because it runs on the laptop where it was created. The
strongest beginner test is intentionally inconvenient: clone it into a fresh directory and
follow only the documented instructions. Hidden local files, global packages, undeclared
environment variables and path assumptions become visible immediately.
Picture it in your head
Imagine handing the repository to an interviewer who has never seen your computer. They
should not need your Downloads folder, your global Python site-packages, a secret hidden in
shell history or an instruction you forgot to write down. The repository should state the start
point, prerequisites, setup, run command, inputs, outputs and validation.
Follow with me once
Take the supplied practice/sample_project as a model only for handoff mechanics, not as
your final evidence. Put your learner-owned project in a Git repository and push to a remote
(GitHub when available, local bare remote is acceptable for mechanics). Then leave the original
folder.
Clone to a genuinely different path:
cd ~/de-study/M06
rm -rf clean-check   # ONLY if this exact disposable folder is yours and inspected
git clone <remote-url-or-local-bare-path> clean-check
cd clean-check
Do not copy your old .venv. Follow README:
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python app.py
For the supplied sample project the independent control is:
source_rows = 6
completed_rows = 4
completed_amount = 3900
Also verify ignored/generated state:
git status --short
A clean-clone run that requires untracked source data from your old machine is a failed handoff
even if the original project still runs.
The handoff defense
You should be able to answer:
• What is the entry point?
• Which files are source vs generated?
• What environment/config must be supplied?
• What should never be committed?
• What exact output/control proves the run worked?
• What happens on invalid/missing input?
